# Camera Trajectory Representations

Also called: Camera trajectory interpolation, SE(3) trajectory parameterization, Trajectory Representations for Camera Motion

## Overview
This family defines the mathematical parameterization of camera motion trajectories used to approximate camera movement during shutter exposure time for [motion blur](#6441-motion-blur.md) synthesis. It solves the problem of how to interpolate between known camera poses to generate intermediate virtual views. The choice of representation is primarily driven by the complexity of the motion and the duration of the exposure: [linear interpolation](#14935-linear-interpolation.md) is sufficient for synthetic scenes with short time intervals, while cubic B-splines are required for real captured scenes with longer exposure times and complex motions.

## Shared principles
All representations in this family operate within the Lie group SE(3) to ensure valid [rigid body transformations](#11475-rigid-body-transformation-se3.md). The core mechanism involves optimizing a set of parameters to define the path between camera poses. The trajectory is typically discretized into $n$ intermediate virtual images to balance rendering performance and training efficiency, with $n=10$ being a common empirical choice [S1]. The optimization targets the camera poses themselves, rather than just the trajectory shape, allowing the model to adapt to the specific blur characteristics of the input data.

## Subtopics

### Linear Interpolation
Linear interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by optimizing only the start pose $\mathbf{T}_{start}$ and the end pose $\mathbf{T}_{end}$. The intermediate poses are generated by linearly interpolating between these two endpoints. This method is computationally efficient and sufficient for synthetic datasets where camera motions are simpler and exposure times are effectively shorter [S1]. It is employed for synthetic datasets such as those from Deblur-NeRF-S and MBA-VO [S1].

### Cubic B-Spline Interpolation
Cubic B-spline interpolation parameterizes the trajectory by jointly optimizing four control knots: $\mathbf{T}_1, \mathbf{T}_2, \mathbf{T}_3,$ and $\mathbf{T}_4$. This higher-order spline allows for the modeling of more complex camera motions and nuances over longer time intervals [S1]. It outperforms linear interpolation in real captured scenes, particularly due to the longer exposure times inherent in real-world image capture [S1]. It is employed for real datasets, such as the 10 real captured scenes from Deblur-NeRF [S1].

## Background
The distinction between linear and higher-order spline representations for camera trajectories in the context of [neural rendering](#6800-neural-rendering.md) and deblurring was formalized in the [BAD-Gaussians](#18036-bad-gaussians.md) paper [S1]. The authors conducted experiments on both synthetic datasets (Deblur-NeRF-S, MBA-VO) and real datasets (Deblur-NeRF) to assess the impact of trajectory representations. They found that while linear interpolation performed comparably to cubic B-splines on synthetic data, the latter was necessary for real data to handle complex motions and longer exposure times effectively. The specific mathematical details of the cubic B-spline implementation are referenced from external literature [S1].
